title: Hoisting
theory: Before executing a scope, JavaScript creates bindings for declarations. A var binding starts as undefined. A function declaration is already callable. let and const bindings exist but cannot be accessed before their declaration executes.
analogy: The room is reserved before you arrive, but a let or const room stays locked until check-in.
answer: Hoisting describes declaration processing before execution. var is initialized to undefined; let and const remain in the temporal dead zone. Function declarations are initialized with their function value.
pitfall: JavaScript does not literally move your source code. Function expressions follow the rules of their variable binding.

title: let, const and var
theory: let and const have block scope. var has function scope and permits redeclaration. let permits reassignment; const prevents reassignment of the binding, but an object stored in const can still be mutated.
analogy: const fixes the label on a box, not everything inside the box.
answer: Prefer const unless reassignment is needed; use let for changing bindings. Avoid var in new code because its function scope and hoisting often surprise readers.
pitfall: const is not deep immutability. Object.freeze is also shallow.

title: map vs forEach
theory: map transforms every item and returns a new array of the same length. forEach performs side effects and returns undefined. Neither automatically mutates the input, but your callback can.
analogy: map creates a new tray of meals; forEach visits each meal to perform an action.
answer: Use map when you need transformed values. Use forEach for side effects. Neither awaits an async callback.
pitfall: For async work use Promise.all(array.map(...)) or a for...of loop with await.

title: filter
theory: filter returns a new array containing the elements whose callback returns a truthy value. It does not change the original array. Object elements are still shared references.
analogy: A gate lets only matching items through.
answer: filter selects items; map transforms items. filter can return fewer items or an empty array.
code:
const users = [{name:'A', active:true}, {name:'B', active:false}];
console.log(users.filter(user => user.active));
starter:
const users = [{name:'A', active:true}, {name:'B', active:false}];
console.log(users.filter(user => user.active));
pitfall: Returning an object from the predicate always counts as truthy.

title: reduce
theory: reduce processes items from left to right while carrying an accumulator. The accumulator can be a number, object or array. Give an initial value to make the behavior clear and handle empty arrays.
analogy: A running bill carries the previous total to the next item.
answer: reduce combines a collection into one result, such as a sum, grouped object or lookup map.
pitfall: Without an initial value, reducing an empty array throws. Avoid copying a large accumulator on every iteration.

title: ES6+ array and object methods
theory: find returns the first matching item; some asks whether any item matches; every asks whether all items match. includes tests membership. Object.entries produces key/value pairs. flat and optional chaining arrived after ES6.
analogy: Choose a tool according to the question: which one, any, all, or contains?
answer: Know what each method returns and whether it mutates. sort, reverse and splice mutate; map, filter, slice and toSorted return new arrays.
pitfall: Default sort compares strings. ES6 is not the name for every modern JavaScript feature.

title: Arrow functions and this
theory: Arrow functions provide compact function syntax and capture this from the surrounding lexical scope. They do not have their own arguments and cannot be constructors.
analogy: An arrow borrows the surrounding room’s identity instead of receiving a new one.
answer: Use arrow callbacks when lexical this is useful. Use a regular method when this should come from the object calling it.
pitfall: call, apply and bind cannot replace the lexical this of an arrow function.

title: IIFE
theory: An immediately invoked function expression runs as soon as it is created. It creates a private scope. Async IIFEs also provide a place to use await in scripts.
analogy: Build a small temporary room, do the job, then close the door.
answer: An IIFE is a function expression followed by invocation parentheses. Modules and block-scoped bindings replace many older IIFE use cases.
pitfall: A leading semicolon can prevent accidental joining with the previous expression.

title: Promises
theory: A promise represents a future result. It begins pending and settles once as fulfilled or rejected. then handles success, catch handles failure and finally performs cleanup without normally replacing the result.
analogy: A restaurant receipt promises a meal later; it is not the meal itself.
answer: Promises make asynchronous results composable. Returning a value or another promise from then determines the next link in the chain.
pitfall: The Promise executor runs synchronously. A promise itself does not make CPU-heavy work run on another thread.

title: async and await
theory: An async function always returns a promise. await pauses that function until the awaited value settles, while other work can continue. Use try/catch for rejections.
analogy: You pause your own order while the kitchen keeps serving other tables.
answer: async/await is promise-based syntax. Independent operations can start together and be awaited with Promise.all.
pitfall: Sequential awaits can unnecessarily serialize independent requests. await does not block the whole JavaScript thread.

title: Event loop and output order
theory: Synchronous code runs on the call stack. Once the stack is empty, queued microtasks such as promise reactions run before the next timer task. Timers specify a minimum delay, not an exact execution time.
analogy: Finish the current customer, clear the priority queue, then serve the next regular ticket.
answer: In this browser example the output is A, D, C, B: synchronous logs, then the promise microtask, then the timer callback.
pitfall: Node has additional scheduling details such as process.nextTick. Do not blindly apply one browser ordering example to every Node context.

title: Shallow copy vs deep copy
theory: Spread and Object.assign copy only the outer level. Nested objects are still shared. structuredClone copies supported nested data into independent objects and supports cycles.
analogy: A shallow copy gives two folders pointing at the same document. A deep copy duplicates the document too.
answer: Use shallow copies for targeted immutable updates. Use structuredClone when you truly need an independent copy of supported data.
pitfall: structuredClone cannot clone functions or DOM nodes and does not preserve custom prototype chains. JSON cloning loses some data types.

title: call, apply and bind
theory: call invokes a function with a chosen this and separate arguments. apply invokes it with an array-like list. bind returns a new function with this and optional arguments fixed.
analogy: call and apply place the call now; bind saves a number for later.
answer: call(obj, a, b) and apply(obj, [a,b]) execute immediately. bind(obj, a) returns a function for later execution.
pitfall: They do not change this for arrow functions.

title: Closures
theory: A function can keep access to variables from its lexical environment even after the outer function has returned. Each call to a factory can create a separate environment.
analogy: A function leaves home carrying a backpack of the variables it can still access.
answer: A closure combines a function and its surrounding lexical environment. Common uses include private state, callbacks, factories and memoization.
pitfall: Closures capture bindings, not frozen snapshots. React callbacks can capture values from an earlier render.

title: Prototype and prototype chain
theory: Objects can delegate missing property lookups to another object, their prototype. The chain continues until a property is found or null is reached. A constructor function’s prototype becomes the prototype of objects created with new.
analogy: If your desk lacks a manual, ask the shared bookshelf, then the main library.
answer: Prototype-based delegation lets instances share behavior without copying methods into each instance.
pitfall: An object’s internal prototype is different from a constructor’s .prototype property.

title: Prototypal inheritance
theory: JavaScript inheritance delegates property access through prototype links. class and extends are convenient syntax built on this model. A child can override a method while using super to reach the parent implementation.
analogy: A new recipe reuses a base recipe and changes just one step.
answer: Inheritance shares behavior through a prototype chain; composition combines independent behaviors and may be simpler for unrelated capabilities.
pitfall: Do not mutate built-in prototypes in application code.

title: Memoization
theory: Memoization stores a function result for a given input and reuses it when that input appears again. It trades memory for reduced computation. It works best with deterministic functions.
analogy: Keep a notebook of solved problems so you do not solve the same one twice.
answer: A useful cache needs an appropriate key, bounded lifetime and invalidation strategy. Memoization is not automatically faster for cheap calculations.
pitfall: This example supports one primitive input. Multiple arguments and object identity need a deliberate key strategy.

title: Higher-order functions
theory: A higher-order function takes another function as an argument, returns a function, or both. This helps separate a reusable operation from the behavior supplied by the caller.
analogy: A reusable machine accepts different tools to do different jobs.
answer: map, filter and function factories are higher-order functions. A callback is the function passed into another function.
pitfall: Higher-order does not mean asynchronous.

title: Debounce
theory: Debouncing waits until calls stop for a chosen delay before running the action. Every new call resets the timer. It is useful for search input and resize handling.
analogy: Wait until a person finishes speaking before replying.
answer: A debounce function remembers a timer in a closure, clears it on each call and schedules the latest invocation.
pitfall: Cancel pending timers on component unmount. Debouncing requests does not prevent older responses from arriving later.

title: Throttling
theory: Throttling limits how frequently an action can run during continuous input. A leading-edge throttle executes immediately, then ignores calls until the interval ends.
analogy: A gate admits at most one visitor per time interval.
answer: Throttle is useful for scroll or pointer updates. Debounce waits for quiet; throttle allows periodic work while activity continues.
pitfall: This is a leading-only throttle. Some applications also need a trailing call.

title: Destructuring
theory: Destructuring extracts values from arrays or properties from objects into bindings. Object patterns use property names; array patterns use positions. Defaults apply when a value is undefined.
analogy: Unpack selected items from a suitcase into named drawers.
answer: Destructuring supports aliases, defaults, nesting and rest. It makes parameter handling and returned tuples easier to read.
pitfall: A default does not replace null. Nested destructuring throws if the expected parent is missing.

title: Spread and rest
theory: Spread expands iterable values into an array or argument list, or copies enumerable own object properties. Rest collects remaining arguments or destructured values into a new container.
analogy: Spread pours things out; rest gathers what remains.
answer: The same three dots mean expansion or collection depending on the position. Object and array spread make shallow copies.
pitfall: Later object properties overwrite earlier ones. Spreading a huge array into a function can exceed argument limits.

title: Event listeners and delegation
theory: addEventListener registers a handler. DOM events usually travel through capture, target and bubble phases. Delegation attaches a listener to a parent and checks which child triggered the event.
analogy: One receptionist handles visitors for many rooms.
answer: Delegation reduces individual listeners and handles dynamically inserted children. Remove listeners using the same function reference and capture option.
pitfall: preventDefault stops a default browser action; stopPropagation stops further propagation. They are different.

title: Generators
theory: A generator function uses function* and can pause with yield. Calling it creates an iterator; each next() resumes until the next yield or completion.
analogy: A book bookmark lets you resume where you stopped.
answer: Generators produce values lazily and implement the iterator protocol. Async generators can await and yield asynchronous values.
pitfall: The final return value is not included by for...of or spread.

title: Currying
theory: Currying transforms a function of multiple arguments into a sequence of one-argument functions. Each function remembers previous arguments through closures.
analogy: Choose a currency first, then provide the amount later.
answer: Currying enables reusable partially configured functions. Partial application fixes some arguments but does not necessarily create a chain of unary functions.
pitfall: Currying and partial application are related but not identical.

title: Equality, coercion and tricky output
theory: Strict equality compares without coercing types. Loose equality uses conversion rules that can be surprising. Object equality compares identity, not matching content. Use explicit conversion when reading input.
analogy: Two identical-looking houses are still different addresses.
answer: Prefer === for predictable comparisons. Object.is handles NaN as equal to itself and distinguishes positive and negative zero.
pitfall: typeof null is object for historical reasons. NaN === NaN is false.

title: What is React? JSX, props and state
theory: React is a library for building interfaces from components. A component describes UI for its current props and state. JSX is syntax transformed into element creation; it is not an HTML string.
analogy: Components are reusable building blocks; props are instructions and state is each block’s memory.
answer: React uses declarative rendering. You describe what to show; React reconciles changes and commits needed updates to the DOM.
pitfall: Props are read-only. Never mutate state and expect React to detect the change.

title: useState and batching
theory: useState stores a value between renders. Its setter requests a render; it does not change the current render’s variable. Updates based on previous state should use the functional form. React can batch updates.
analogy: Each render is a photograph. Requesting a new photograph does not change the old one.
answer: Use setCount(c => c + 1) for queued updates derived from previous state. React 18 expanded automatic batching with modern roots.
pitfall: Two setCount(count + 1) calls in one event use the same captured count.

title: useEffect and cleanup
theory: Effects synchronize a component with external systems after commits. Dependencies describe reactive values used by the effect. Cleanup runs before the next setup when dependencies change and on unmount.
analogy: Subscribe when you enter a room; unsubscribe when leaving or changing rooms.
answer: Use effects for subscriptions, timers or external integration, not for values you can calculate while rendering. In development Strict Mode can run an extra setup/cleanup cycle.
pitfall: Do not make the effect callback async. Define an async function inside it and handle cleanup/races.

title: useRef
theory: useRef keeps a mutable object across renders. Changing ref.current does not trigger a render. Use refs for DOM nodes, timer IDs or values that are not directly displayed.
analogy: A private sticky note persists without updating the display board.
answer: State controls visible UI; refs hold mutable values outside React’s rendering flow.
pitfall: Avoid reading or writing refs during render except predictable initialization.

title: useContext
theory: Context lets descendants read a provided value without passing it through every intermediate component. Consumers subscribe to context changes. Context is a delivery mechanism; state still lives in a provider or another store.
analogy: A building announcement reaches every subscribing room.
answer: Use context for shared concerns such as theme or current user. Split contexts and stabilize values when unnecessary consumer updates are costly.
pitfall: memo does not prevent a consumer from receiving a changed context value.

title: useReducer
theory: useReducer moves state transitions into a reducer function. Dispatch an action describing what happened; the reducer returns the next state. It is useful for related fields and multi-step updates.
analogy: Send a labeled request to a clerk who follows consistent update rules.
answer: A reducer must be pure. Return a new state and keep side effects outside the reducer.
pitfall: useReducer does not create a global store by itself.

title: useMemo
theory: useMemo caches the result of a calculation between renders while dependencies stay equal by Object.is. It helps avoid expensive recalculation or stabilize a value passed to a memoized child.
analogy: Save a calculation on scratch paper until its inputs change.
answer: useMemo is a performance optimization, not a correctness guarantee. Profile first and keep calculations pure.
pitfall: Do not use useMemo for side effects or omit dependencies to force caching.

title: useCallback and React.memo
theory: useCallback caches a function identity while its dependencies stay the same. memo can skip rendering a component when its props are unchanged. Neither makes all rendering free.
analogy: Give a child the same instruction card instead of printing an identical new one.
answer: useCallback is most useful with memoized consumers or dependencies that care about function identity. Measure the actual bottleneck.
pitfall: A memoized component still rerenders for its own state or consumed context updates.

title: useLayoutEffect
theory: useLayoutEffect runs after DOM changes but before the browser paints. It is useful when measuring layout must happen before displaying the result. It can block painting, so prefer useEffect otherwise.
analogy: Adjust the stage before the curtain opens.
answer: Use layout effects sparingly for measurements or visual positioning that would otherwise flicker.
pitfall: Effects do not run during server rendering.

title: useId · React 18
theory: useId creates a stable ID for accessibility relationships such as labels and inputs. It supports consistent server/client IDs when the component tree matches.
analogy: A matching ticket connects the label to the correct input.
answer: Use useId for accessibility attributes. Use IDs from your data for list keys.
code:
import {useId} from 'react';
export default function App(){const id=useId();return <><label htmlFor={id}>Email </label><input id={id} type='email'/></>;}
starter:
import {useId} from 'react';
export default function App(){const id=useId();return <><label htmlFor={id}>Email </label><input id={id} type='email'/></>;}
pitfall: Do not use useId to generate list keys.

title: useTransition · React 18
theory: useTransition marks updates as non-urgent and exposes isPending. React can keep urgent interactions responsive while preparing the transition. The callback itself is invoked immediately.
analogy: Typing goes in the express lane; a large results update can wait.
answer: Use transitions for non-urgent rendering updates. A transition is not a debounce, timer or background JavaScript thread.
pitfall: Do not transition the state that directly controls a text input.

title: useDeferredValue · React 18
theory: useDeferredValue lets a part of the UI lag behind a changing value so urgent updates can render first. React attempts the background render when it can.
analogy: The search field responds now while the results board catches up.
answer: Defer a value when you do not control its setter. Unlike debounce, it has no fixed time delay and does not reduce network requests by itself.
code:
import {useState,useDeferredValue} from 'react'; export default function App(){const [text,setText]=useState('');const deferred=useDeferredValue(text);return <>setText(e.target.value)}/>

Results for {deferred}

;}

Results for {deferred}

;}
pitfall: Memoize expensive children when appropriate so the urgent render can skip their work.

title: useSyncExternalStore · React 18
theory: This hook subscribes to state stored outside React. Supply a subscribe function and a stable snapshot reader. An optional server snapshot supports server rendering.
analogy: React subscribes to another system’s notice board.
answer: Library authors use this API to keep external-store subscriptions consistent with concurrent rendering.
pitfall: Returning a newly created snapshot object on every call can cause repeated updates.

title: useInsertionEffect · React 18
theory: useInsertionEffect is designed for CSS-in-JS library authors to insert styles before layout effects read layout. Most application components should not use it.
analogy: Install the stylesheet before measuring the stage.
answer: This is a specialized library hook, not a faster replacement for useEffect. Refs may not yet be attached and state updates are not allowed inside it.
code:
import {useInsertionEffect} from 'react'; export default function App(){useInsertionEffect(()=>{const style=document.createElement('style');style.textContent='.demo{color:teal}';document.head.appendChild(style);return()=>style.remove();},[]);return

Style inserted

;}

Style inserted

;}
pitfall: Prefer normal CSS files for application styles.

title: useImperativeHandle
theory: useImperativeHandle defines what a parent receives through a ref. Expose a small API, such as focus, instead of an entire DOM node. React 19 supports ref as a prop; older versions use forwardRef.
analogy: Expose a few buttons on a machine rather than its internal wiring.
answer: Use imperative handles only for behaviors that cannot be conveniently expressed with props.
pitfall: Keep the exposed API small. This example uses React 19 ref-as-prop.

title: useDebugValue
theory: useDebugValue adds a label for a custom hook in React DevTools. It does not render visible UI. It is most useful for shared hooks whose internal state is hard to inspect.
analogy: Attach a maintenance label that developers can read.
answer: Use useDebugValue inside a custom hook and optionally supply a formatter to avoid expensive label formatting on every render.
pitfall: The label appears in React DevTools, not in the page.

title: useActionState · React 19
theory: useActionState connects an action to its result state and pending status. The action receives the previous state plus its payload. Passing the action to a form provides the action context.
analogy: A form keeps the result of its latest submitted request.
answer: It returns [state, dispatchAction, isPending]. Handle expected validation errors by returning a useful state; protect real mutations on the server.
pitfall: The first action argument is previous state, so the FormData argument comes second.

title: useOptimistic · React 19
theory: useOptimistic shows a temporary result while an action is pending. When the action finishes, the UI uses the confirmed state. It can make operations feel immediate while still handling failure.
analogy: Display the draft change while waiting for the receipt.
answer: Use an optimistic reducer and dispatch inside an Action or transition. Save the authoritative result separately and show useful errors if the request fails.
code:
import {useState,useOptimistic,startTransition} from 'react';
export default function App(){const [count,setCount]=useState(0);const [optimistic,add]=useOptimistic(count,(n,amount)=>n+amount);return <button onClick={()=>startTransition(async()=>{add(1);await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,600));startTransition(()=>setCount(n=>n+1));})}>Likes {optimistic}{optimistic!==count?' · saving':''}</button>;}
starter:
import {useState,useOptimistic,startTransition} from 'react';
export default function App(){const [count,setCount]=useState(0);const [optimistic,add]=useOptimistic(count,(n,amount)=>n+amount);return <button onClick={()=>startTransition(async()=>{add(1);await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,600));startTransition(()=>setCount(n=>n+1));})}>Likes {optimistic}{optimistic!==count?' · saving':''}</button>;}
pitfall: Optimistic state is temporary. Do not treat it as a confirmed server write.

title: useFormStatus · React 19
theory: useFormStatus from react-dom reads the status of the nearest parent form submission. Place the consuming component inside the form. It returns pending and submission-related information.
analogy: A submit button reads the status light of the form it belongs to.
answer: Use a nested submit-button component to show pending state without manually threading props.
pitfall: Calling useFormStatus in the component that creates the form does not read that form’s status.

title: use API · React 19
theory: use reads a resource such as a promise or context. Reading a pending promise suspends rendering and works with Suspense. Unlike ordinary hooks, use can be called in conditions or loops, but only inside a component or hook.
analogy: A component waits behind a loading curtain until its resource arrives.
answer: For client promise reads, use stable promises supplied by a cache or framework. Creating a new promise on every render leads to repeated suspension.
pitfall: use is a React API with special rules, not simply an alias for await.

title: useEffectEvent · React 19.2
theory: useEffectEvent extracts non-reactive logic from an effect while letting it read the latest committed props and state. It is useful for events caused by an external subscription.
analogy: An effect keeps its subscription but reads today’s notice when an event occurs.
answer: Call Effect Events from effects, not click handlers. They are not an escape hatch for suppressing legitimate effect dependencies.
code:
import {useState,useEffect,useEffectEvent} from 'react';
export default function App(){const [name,setName]=useState('Kri');const onTick=useEffectEvent(()=>console.log('Latest name:',name));useEffect(()=>{const id=setInterval(()=>onTick(),2000);return()=>clearInterval(id);},[]);return <input value={name} onChange={e=>setName(e.target.value)}/>;}
starter:
import {useState,useEffect,useEffectEvent} from 'react';
export default function App(){const [name,setName]=useState('Kri');const onTick=useEffectEvent(()=>console.log('Latest name:',name));useEffect(()=>{const id=setInterval(()=>onTick(),2000);return()=>clearInterval(id);},[]);return <input value={name} onChange={e=>setName(e.target.value)}/>;}
pitfall: This hook requires React 19.2 or later, not React 19.0.

title: Custom hooks and Rules of Hooks
theory: A custom hook is a function beginning with use that composes hooks to share stateful logic. Each caller gets its own state unless the hook explicitly connects to shared state. Call ordinary hooks at the top level.
analogy: Two houses can use the same blueprint without sharing the same kitchen.
answer: Extract behavior into custom hooks when it is reused or clarifies a component. Do not call hooks conditionally, in loops or in regular callbacks.
pitfall: Sharing a custom hook does not automatically share its state between components.

title: Higher-order components (HOC)
theory: An HOC is a function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component. It can inject props or wrap behavior. Custom hooks often share logic more directly in modern function components.
analogy: Wrap a plain gift with reusable packaging.
answer: HOCs are composition patterns, not a separate React API. Preserve component props and create the enhanced component outside rendering.
pitfall: Creating an HOC inside a component produces a new component type and can reset state.

title: Redux and Redux Toolkit
theory: Redux is an external store with predictable state transitions. Components dispatch actions; reducers compute the next state; selectors read values. Redux Toolkit reduces boilerplate and is the standard way to write Redux.
analogy: A central records office accepts requests and publishes updated records.
answer: Use Redux for complex shared client state when its structure and tooling help. Context distributes values; Redux adds store conventions, middleware and debugging tools.
pitfall: Toolkit reducers use Immer drafts. Mutating ordinary React state is still incorrect.

title: Redux Thunk and async actions
theory: Thunk middleware allows dispatching functions that receive dispatch and getState. The function can perform async work and then dispatch plain actions. Redux Toolkit includes thunk middleware by default.
analogy: An assistant performs the long-running errand, then files the result at the records office.
answer: createAsyncThunk generates pending, fulfilled and rejected actions. RTK Query is often a better fit for standard server-data fetching and caching.
pitfall: Do not put side effects inside reducers.

title: Class lifecycle vs function components
theory: Classes organize side effects around mount, update and unmount methods. Functions organize synchronization around effects and dependencies. An effect is not a perfect one-to-one replacement for each lifecycle method.
analogy: Classes group work by time; effects group work by the external system being synchronized.
answer: componentDidMount roughly maps to effect setup, componentWillUnmount to cleanup, and componentDidUpdate to dependency-driven reruns. useState/useReducer replace class state; refs replace mutable instance fields.
code:
import {useEffect,useState} from 'react';
export default function App(){const [room,setRoom]=useState('A');useEffect(()=>{console.log('Connect',room);return()=>console.log('Disconnect',room);},[room]);return <button onClick={()=>setRoom(r=>r==='A'?'B':'A')}>Room {room}</button>;}
starter:

export default function App(){const [room,setRoom]=useState('A');useEffect(()=>{console.log('Connect',room);return()=>console.log('Disconnect',room);},[room]);return <button onClick={()=>setRoom(r=>r==='A'?'B':'A')}>Room {room}</button>;}
pitfall: Render must stay pure. Error boundary lifecycle APIs still commonly require a class or a library.

title: Keys, reconciliation and controlled inputs
theory: Keys tell React which list items retain identity across renders. Stable data IDs preserve local state through reordering. A controlled input gets value and onChange from React state.
analogy: A name badge tracks the person even when the seating order changes.
answer: Use stable unique sibling keys. Controlled inputs are convenient for validation and synchronized UI; uncontrolled inputs can be read with refs or FormData.

title: Performance optimization and Suspense
theory: First measure slow interactions with browser tools and the React Profiler. Keep state close to where it is used, avoid unnecessary effects, virtualize huge lists and lazy-load large features. Memoize only when it helps.
analogy: Find the traffic jam before adding more roads.
answer: Suspense coordinates loading boundaries for compatible resources such as lazy components. It does not automatically detect fetching started in useEffect.
pitfall: This runnable example simulates a dynamic import. In a real app use lazy(() => import("./Detail")).

title: What is Next.js? App Router
theory: Next.js is a React framework that adds routing, rendering options, server features and build tooling. In the App Router, folders define route segments and page.tsx defines a page. layout.tsx wraps related routes.
analogy: React supplies the building blocks; Next.js supplies the building’s routing and infrastructure.
answer: Choose Next.js when integrated server rendering, routing and server features fit the application. React alone does not prescribe these features.
pitfall: A React component running in this dashboard is not a real Next.js server runtime.

title: SSR · server-side rendering
theory: SSR generates HTML using request-time information on the server. It can support personalized or frequently changing content. The browser can display HTML before interactive components finish loading.
analogy: Cook a fresh meal for each order.
answer: SSR favors freshness and request-specific data but requires server work for requests. In the Pages Router getServerSideProps runs for each request.
pitfall: SSR does not mean there is no client JavaScript. Interactive components still need hydration.

title: SSG · static site generation
theory: SSG creates reusable HTML ahead of requests, often during a build. It is good for content shared by many visitors that does not need request-time personalization.
analogy: Prepare meals ahead of the lunch rush.
answer: SSG offers fast reusable output and lower request-time work. Content changes require rebuilding or a revalidation strategy.
pitfall: Do not put user-specific secrets in generated pages or serialized props.

title: ISR · incremental static regeneration
theory: ISR serves a cached static page and updates it without rebuilding the whole site. Time-based revalidation makes a page eligible for regeneration; it is not a precise timer job. The usual abbreviation is ISR, not ISG.
analogy: Serve the prepared menu while the kitchen refreshes the next batch.
answer: ISR combines reusable output with periodic or on-demand freshness. A stale request can trigger background regeneration while the previous page is served.
pitfall: ISR requires a compatible server platform; a plain static export does not provide runtime regeneration.

title: Server Components vs Client Components
theory: App Router components are Server Components by default. They can read server data and avoid sending their component code to the browser. Add use client at an entry boundary for state, effects or browser events.
analogy: The kitchen prepares data; the dining-room controls respond to the customer.
answer: Client Components may still be prerendered on the server. use client marks a client module boundary, not an instruction to render exclusively in the browser.
pitfall: Props crossing the server/client boundary must be serializable by React. Never expose server secrets in client modules.

title: Hydration and streaming
theory: Hydration attaches client behavior to server-generated markup. The first client render must match the server output. Streaming sends ready pieces of UI while slower Suspense boundaries are still resolving.
analogy: Open completed rooms while workers finish the remaining rooms.
answer: Use stable initial output and loading boundaries. Read browser-only values after mounting or intentionally disable SSR for an appropriate client-only feature.
pitfall: Random numbers, dates and browser-specific branches during initial render commonly cause hydration mismatches.

title: Dynamic routes, layouts and navigation
theory: A segment such as [id] matches a dynamic path. Layouts persist shared UI across navigation. Link performs framework-aware navigation and can prefetch eligible destinations.
analogy: A shared hallway leads to different numbered rooms.
answer: Use route segments for URL structure, layouts for shared shells and search parameters for shareable filters. Current App Router params are asynchronous.
pitfall: Do not copy Pages Router router APIs into App Router code; use next/navigation there.

title: Caching and revalidation
theory: Caching rules vary by router, framework version and whether Cache Components is enabled. Choose caching explicitly and distinguish data cache, rendered output and browser navigation cache.
analogy: A library has several shelves with separate refresh policies.
answer: Understand your configured model before choosing APIs. The included local example uses the Pages Router ISR contract for clarity; the App Router also supports newer Cache Components APIs.
pitfall: Do not combine no-store with a positive revalidate option. Check current docs for Cache Components configuration.

title: Route handlers and Server Actions
theory: Route handlers implement HTTP endpoints using Request and Response. Server Actions run server-side functions used for mutations. Both must validate input and enforce authentication and authorization.
analogy: An endpoint is a service desk; an action is a specific submitted request.
answer: Use route.ts for HTTP APIs and server actions for supported mutation flows. Revalidate affected content after a successful mutation when needed.
pitfall: use server is not authorization. Do not trust input merely because it came from your own UI.

title: SEO, metadata and image optimization
theory: Next.js supports route metadata and optimized image components. Metadata describes a page to search engines and link previews. Image sizing helps reserve layout space and avoid jumps.
analogy: Label the book clearly and reserve space for its illustrations.
answer: Provide meaningful titles and descriptions. Use next/image with dimensions or a correctly sized fill container and configured remote sources.
pitfall: Server rendering alone does not guarantee good SEO; semantic content, performance and crawlability matter.

title: What is Node.js?
theory: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, using V8 plus runtime APIs for networking, files and processes. It is well suited to I/O-heavy services.
analogy: One coordinator delegates slow I/O rather than waiting at each desk.
answer: Node executes JavaScript callbacks on an event-loop thread by default; the runtime also uses operating-system facilities and a worker pool.
code:
console.log('Runtime:', process.version);
console.log('Platform:', process.platform);
starter:
console.log('Runtime:', process.version);
console.log('Platform:', process.platform);
pitfall: Node is not a framework. CPU-heavy JavaScript still blocks its current thread.

title: Event loop, libuv and non-blocking I/O
theory: Node starts asynchronous I/O and later runs completion callbacks. libuv provides event-loop machinery and a worker pool for selected operations. Not every asynchronous API uses a pool thread.
analogy: A coordinator sends work out and responds when results arrive.
answer: Avoid synchronous heavy work in request handlers. Use worker threads for suitable CPU-heavy JavaScript; asynchronous I/O is different from CPU parallelism.
pitfall: The order of setTimeout and setImmediate depends on context; do not promise one universal order.

title: ES modules vs CommonJS
theory: ES modules use import/export. CommonJS uses require/module.exports. Node interprets .mjs as ESM and .cjs as CommonJS; package.json type controls .js defaults.
analogy: Two packaging systems use different labels and loading rules.
answer: Choose one module system deliberately and understand interoperability. In ESM use import.meta.url instead of assuming __dirname exists.
pitfall: A browser cannot execute node: imports. Use the included local Node examples.

title: Build an HTTP server
theory: The built-in http module can receive requests and send responses without Express. You must handle routing, status codes, headers and request parsing yourself.
analogy: A receptionist checks the requested room and sends a reply.
answer: Frameworks add routing and middleware conveniences; they are not required to serve HTTP.
pitfall: Set response headers before writing the body and always end the response.

title: Middleware and error handling
theory: Middleware is a chain of request-processing functions. Each step can attach data, respond or pass control. Centralized error handling turns failures into consistent responses.
analogy: A request moves through reception, identity checks and the service desk.
answer: Order matters. Parse input, authenticate, authorize, validate and run business logic; send a controlled error response for failures.
pitfall: Do not expose stack traces or secrets in public error responses.

title: Streams and backpressure
theory: Streams process data in chunks so the entire file need not be loaded into memory. Backpressure slows the producer when the consumer cannot keep up.
analogy: Pour water at the speed the funnel can accept.
answer: Use pipeline to connect streams and propagate errors. Streaming improves memory behavior for large files and responses.
pitfall: Ignoring write() returning false can cause excessive buffering.

title: Buffer and binary data
theory: Buffer stores bytes and helps process files, network data and encoded content. A string represents text; converting bytes to text requires an encoding.
analogy: Bytes are raw ingredients; decoding turns them into readable text.
answer: Use Buffer.from for existing content and Buffer.alloc for initialized storage. Understand UTF-8 versus base64.
pitfall: A character can occupy multiple bytes in UTF-8.

title: EventEmitter
theory: EventEmitter implements named in-process events. Listeners registered with on run synchronously when emit is called. once handles only the next occurrence.
analogy: Ring a bell and all current listeners react.
answer: Use events to decouple local components; they are not a durable cross-service message queue.
pitfall: An emitted error event without a handler can terminate the process.

title: Worker threads vs cluster
theory: Worker threads run JavaScript in parallel threads and can share memory. Multiple processes have separate memory and can distribute server load. Choose according to the bottleneck.
analogy: More cooks help CPU work; more independent kitchens serve separate crowds.
answer: Workers suit CPU-intensive tasks. They usually do not improve ordinary asynchronous I/O enough to justify their overhead.
pitfall: Use worker pools for repeated tasks; spawning a worker per tiny job is expensive.

title: Authentication, authorization and JWT
theory: Authentication identifies a user; authorization checks allowed actions. A signed JWT can carry claims, but signing does not encrypt them. Validate signature, issuer, audience and expiry.
analogy: A badge says who you are; access rules decide which doors open.
answer: Choose a deliberate session or token design. Keep credentials and signing secrets on the server, use HTTPS and enforce authorization for every protected operation.
pitfall: Decoding a JWT without verifying it does not authenticate a request.

title: REST APIs, validation and status codes
theory: REST-style APIs model resources using URLs and HTTP methods. Validate types and limits at the boundary. Use status codes that describe the result rather than returning 200 for every outcome.
analogy: Each service desk has a clear request form and result receipt.
answer: GET reads, POST usually creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates and DELETE removes. Use 201 for creation, 400 for invalid input and 404 for absent resources.
pitfall: Validation is not authorization. Parameterize SQL instead of concatenating input.

title: Environment variables and configuration
theory: Read configuration from the environment so code can run in different environments without edits. Validate required values at startup and keep secrets out of source control.
analogy: One appliance uses different settings in each room.
answer: Use process.env, explicit defaults and fail-fast validation. Environment values are strings or undefined, so parse numbers and booleans carefully.
pitfall: Frontend environment variables are often bundled publicly. Do not place secrets there.

title: Testing APIs and graceful shutdown
theory: Test successful and failing requests and close resources when shutting down. node:test and node:assert can validate behavior without a testing framework.
analogy: Check both working doors and locked doors, then close the building safely.
answer: Separate pure logic from network setup so it is easy to test. On shutdown stop accepting requests and close database connections with a bounded timeout.
pitfall: A running timer, server or database pool can keep tests and processes alive.

title: package.json vs package-lock.json
theory: package.json declares project scripts, metadata and dependency ranges. package-lock.json records the resolved dependency tree so installs can reproduce it.
analogy: A shopping list versus the exact receipt.
answer: Commit both files. npm install can update resolution; npm ci installs from the lockfile and fails when it disagrees with package.json.
pitfall: Do not manually edit the lockfile to resolve a dependency issue.

title: npm vs npx
theory: npm manages packages and runs scripts. npx, implemented through npm exec, executes a package command, using a local installation when available or obtaining one when needed.
analogy: npm stocks the toolbox; npx runs a tool.
answer: Use npm run for project scripts and npx for package CLIs. Pin versions for reproducible one-off commands.
code:
npm install
npm run dev
npx tsc --noEmit
starter:
npm install
npm run dev
npx tsc --noEmit
pitfall: npx can download and execute code. Verify the package and command.

title: Axios vs fetch
theory: fetch is a standard web API and Axios is a client library. fetch resolves on HTTP error responses, so check response.ok. Axios rejects non-success status codes by default and provides interceptors and transforms.
analogy: Both deliver the parcel, with different built-in handling.
answer: Use fetch for a small native dependency footprint; use Axios when its conventions and features fit. Handle cancellation, errors and timeouts deliberately.
pitfall: fetch rejects for network failures, not automatically for 404 or 500.

title: useQuery · TanStack Query
theory: useQuery manages cached server state with loading, errors, refetching and deduplication. The query key identifies the data; every changing input used by the query should be represented in that key.
analogy: A shared notebook avoids fetching the same answer repeatedly.
answer: Provide a QueryClientProvider and use the object options API. staleTime controls freshness; gcTime controls retention of inactive cached data.
code:
import {useQuery} from '@tanstack/react-query';
function useUser(id){return useQuery({queryKey:['user',id],queryFn:async()=>{const r=await fetch('/api/users/'+id);if(!r.ok)throw new Error('Failed');return r.json();},enabled:!!id,staleTime:60000});}
starter:
import {useQuery} from '@tanstack/react-query';
function useUser(id){return useQuery({queryKey:['user',id],queryFn:async()=>{const r=await fetch('/api/users/'+id);if(!r.ok)throw new Error('Failed');return r.json();},enabled:!!id,staleTime:60000});}
pitfall: Server state caching is different from local UI state. This example needs TanStack Query and a provider.

title: GraphQL vs REST
theory: GraphQL lets clients request selected fields through a schema. Resolvers supply those fields from databases, REST services or other sources. Queries read data; mutations request changes.
analogy: Order selected dishes from a typed menu instead of accepting a fixed platter.
answer: GraphQL is not a database or a replacement for the HTTP server runtime. A Java or Node backend must expose a GraphQL schema and resolvers to support GraphQL queries.
pitfall: A GraphQL client cannot arbitrarily filter an existing REST response on the server unless a GraphQL layer is implemented.

title: TypeScript types, interfaces and generics
theory: TypeScript checks JavaScript code before it runs. Interfaces describe object shapes; type aliases can also describe unions and other type expressions. Generics preserve relationships between input and output types.
analogy: Check the blueprint before building; still inspect real deliveries at runtime.
answer: Use unknown for untrusted values and narrow it. Static types do not validate API payloads at runtime.
pitfall: Avoid any when it merely hides an error. Type annotations disappear during compilation.

title: Remove duplicates
theory: Return unique primitive values while preserving their first appearance.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Set stores distinct primitive values. Spreading it creates an array. Expected: [1, 2, 3]. Average O(n) time and O(n) extra space.
code:
function unique(values){return [...new Set(values)];}
console.log(unique([1,2,2,3,1]));
pitfall: Objects are deduplicated by reference, not matching properties.

title: Find the second largest unique value
theory: Return the second largest distinct number, or null if fewer than two distinct values exist.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Track the largest and second largest distinct values in one pass. Expected: 7. O(n) time, O(1) extra space for finite numbers.
pitfall: This implementation assumes finite numeric inputs; validate inputs in production.

title: Group objects by property
theory: Group employees into an object keyed by department.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Accumulate an array for each key. A null-prototype accumulator avoids inherited property name collisions. Average O(n) time.
pitfall: The objects themselves are still the original references.

title: Flatten an array (flat array): recursion and flat()
theory: Flatten an arbitrarily nested array of values.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Recursively visit each nested array. Expected: [1,2,3,4]. flat(Infinity) is the built-in alternative.
pitfall: Very deep recursion can overflow the stack; huge spread argument lists also have limits.

title: Two sum
theory: Return indices of two numbers that add to a target; return an empty array if there is no pair.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Store previously seen numbers and their indices. Look up the needed complement before inserting the current number. Expected: [0,1]. Average O(n) time.
code:
function twoSum(nums,target){const seen=new Map();for(let i=0;i<nums.length;i++){const needed=target-nums[i];if(seen.has(needed))return [seen.get(needed),i];seen.set(nums[i],i);}return [];}
console.log(twoSum([2,7,11,15],9));
pitfall: Do not use the same index twice.

title: Count occurrences
theory: Count how many times each word appears.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Increment a counter per key. Expected: react: 2 and node: 1. A Map also works for arbitrary key types.
code:
function frequencies(words){const result=Object.create(null);for(const word of words)result[word]=(result[word]??0)+1;return result;}
console.log(frequencies(['react','node','react']));
pitfall: Normal object keys are strings or symbols; use Map for object keys.

title: Immutable nested update
theory: Update profile.city without changing the original user.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Copy each level on the changed path. Unchanged branches can remain shared. Expected: original Atlanta, updated Hyderabad, equality false.
pitfall: Copying only the outer object leaves profile shared.

title: Convert pairs into an object
theory: Create an object from key/value pairs and invert it for unique values.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: fromEntries turns pairs into an object. entries performs the reverse operation; map can swap each pair.
starter:
const pairs=[['js','JavaScript'],['ts','TypeScript']];
// Convert and invert
pitfall: Duplicate keys overwrite earlier values; inversion is lossy if values are not unique.

title: Palindrome checker
theory: Ignore case and non-alphanumeric ASCII characters, then check whether the string reads the same backwards.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Normalize first, then compare with the reversed string. Expected: true. O(n) time and space.
code:
function isPalindrome(text){const clean=text.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g,'');return clean===[...clean].reverse().join('');}
console.log(isPalindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'));
pitfall: This exercise specifies ASCII normalization; language-aware Unicode handling needs a different policy.

title: First non-repeating character
theory: Return the first character appearing exactly once, or null.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Count in one pass, then scan again in original order. Expected: w. O(n) time.
code:
function firstUnique(text){const counts=new Map();for(const ch of text)counts.set(ch,(counts.get(ch)??0)+1);for(const ch of text)if(counts.get(ch)===1)return ch;return null;}
console.log(firstUnique('swiss'));
pitfall: for...of handles Unicode code points, not every multi-code-point grapheme.

title: Check anagrams
theory: Check whether two lowercase ASCII words contain the same characters with the same counts.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Increment counts from the first word, decrement while scanning the second. Expected: true. O(n) time.
code:
function anagram(a,b){if(a.length!==b.length)return false;const count=new Map();for(const ch of a)count.set(ch,(count.get(ch)??0)+1);for(const ch of b){if(!count.get(ch))return false;count.set(ch,count.get(ch)-1);}return true;}
console.log(anagram('listen','silent'));
pitfall: Specify whether whitespace, accents and case should be normalized.

title: Reverse words
theory: Trim extra whitespace and reverse word order.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Split by runs of whitespace, reverse the words and join with one space. Expected: today React learn.
code:
function reverseWords(text){return text.trim().split(/\s+/).reverse().join(' ');}
console.log(reverseWords('  learn   React today  '));
pitfall: Reversing words is different from reversing characters.

title: Promise.all vs allSettled
theory: Run two successful jobs and one failed job. Compare all and allSettled.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: all rejects when an input rejects; allSettled waits for every settlement and returns status records. Results retain input order.
starter:
const jobs=[Promise.resolve('A'),Promise.reject(new Error('B failed')),Promise.resolve('C')];
// Handle both methods without unhandled rejections
pitfall: Promise.all does not cancel the other operations when it rejects.

title: Retry a failing async operation
theory: Retry a task up to three total attempts, then throw the final error.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Use a loop with try/await/catch. Return immediately on success and rethrow on the final failure.
pitfall: Real retries should use backoff and only retry safe or idempotent operations.

title: Sequential vs parallel promises
theory: Run three independent async jobs concurrently and retain input order.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: map starts each operation immediately; Promise.all waits for all results in input order. Expected: [2,4,6].
starter:
const job=n=>new Promise(resolve=>setTimeout(()=>resolve(n*2),100));
// Run jobs 1,2,3 together and print results
pitfall: Concurrency can overwhelm a server for huge lists; add a concurrency limit when needed.

title: Promise.race timeout
theory: Reject if an operation takes longer than a timeout and clear the timer afterward.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Race the operation against a rejecting timer. finally clears the timer on either outcome.
code:
async function withTimeout(promise,ms){let timer;try{return await Promise.race([promise,new Promise((_,reject)=>{timer=setTimeout(()=>reject(new Error('Timed out')),ms);})]);}finally{clearTimeout(timer);}}
console.log(await withTimeout(Promise.resolve('Ready'),100));
pitfall: A timeout wrapper does not cancel the underlying operation; use AbortController for supported APIs.

title: Fetch a list → table, search, filter and pagination
theory: Fetch a user list, show it in a table, search by name or email, filter by company and paginate the filtered result. Include loading, error, retry and empty states. Start with local sample JSON, then choose the live demo API to practice a real HTTP request.
analogy: Fetch the full list first. Search and filters narrow it down; pagination chooses which slice of the matching list to display.
answer: Keep fetched data, request status, search, filter and page state separate. useEffect starts the request; AbortController and an active flag prevent obsolete results from updating state. Filter before paginating, reset the page when criteria change, clamp page bounds and use stable IDs for table rows.
pitfall: The local sample uses a Blob URL and still calls fetch/response.json. The live demo needs internet and may fail; use Retry or switch back to sample data. Never paginate before filtering. Do not make the effect callback async.

title: Increment, decrement and reset counter
theory: Build a counter with +, − and reset. Use functional state updates.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: useState stores the value; functional updates always receive the queued previous value.

{count}

pitfall: Keep state immutable and give every interactive control an accessible label.

analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Filter first, then paginate. Reset page to 1 when the query changes so the current page cannot become invalid.
pitfall: Keep state immutable and give every interactive control an accessible label.

theory: Use context to share cart count between a product button and a header.
analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: The provider owns state. Header and Product consume the same context value without prop drilling.

analogy: Try the starter first. Predict the result, run your solution, then compare it with the answer.
answer: Cleanup cancels the old timer whenever inputs change or the component unmounts.
